title: Influence of filler metal features on the fatigue crack growth behavior of high-strength structural steels and their welded joints
abstract: Abstract Nowadays, high-strength steels are becoming increasingly important because of their beneficial properties and versatility. Due to advanced manufacturing technologies, steels with yield strengths of up to 1300 MPa can be produced for thick plates, although their application remains limited. High-strength steels are usually joined by welding, but the strength of the filler metals may be lower than that of the steels themselves. Above 1100 MPa of yield strength, there is no matching type of filler metal so that matching filler metals cannot always be used. High-strength steels are also often subjected to cyclic loading, which can lead to fatigue failure of structural elements or entire structures. In this research, to investigate the effect of the filler metal, different high-strength structural steels (with varying strengths and manufacturing methods) from the 700–1300 MPa strength category were welded using different filler metals from various strength categories, and fatigue crack propagation tests were performed. In addition, on the different base materials, fatigue crack propagation tests were also carried out. In order to obtain more comprehensive results, the position and orientation of the notches were also varied. After the tests, the two parameters ( C  and  n ) of the Paris–Erdogan equation were determined for each specimen using the least squares regression method. The results were compared for the different cases based on the Paris–Erdogan exponents, applying statistical methods. According to the Paris–Erdogan exponent and constant, the relationship was found to be close and reliable for both the base materials and welded joints. The tested steels and their welded joints behaved differently in the longitudinal or transversal directions compared to the thickness direction. The mismatch effect was significant in the investigated directions.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Recent advancements in steel production technologies have enabled the manufacturing of ultrahigh-strength steels suitable for demanding applications such as construction cranes, boom trucks, and other heavy-duty components. Currently—in the case of thick plates—structural steels with yield strengths reaching up to 1300 MPa are available. These high-strength steels offer significant advantages, including increased load-bearing capacity, enhanced wear resistance, and improved machinability [ 1 ,  2 ,  3 ,  4 – 5 ]. Their application can contribute to a substantial reduction in structural self-weight, which in turn lowers handling, fabrication, and transportation costs, as well as overall assembly time [ 6 ]. The relatively low self-weight of ultrahigh-strength steel structures results in significant stress fluctuations under live loads. Consequently, fatigue performance becomes a critical design factor for ensuring structural integrity during service [ 1 ]. Welded components typically exhibit reduced fatigue strength compared to their base materials, largely due to local stress concentrations caused by weld geometry (e.g., notches) and residual tensile stresses induced during cooling and solidification. This degradation in fatigue resistance is a leading cause of failure in welded structures [ 7 ].

Several models exist to describe fatigue crack propagation, none of which enable a fully quantitative treatment of fatigue crack growth. Therefore, semiempirical and/or empirical relationships are generally used, often accompanied by specific crack growth laws. Given that cyclic loads can essentially be of two types—constant or variable amplitude—and that the latter includes single or periodic overloads, as well as stepwise, block, and random loadings, the situation becomes even more complex. It is no coincidence that several attempts have been made to review and compile the various crack growth laws [ 8 ,  9 – 10 ]. Considering that the theoretical description of different loadings, their effects on structures, and their material testing methodologies differ fundamentally [ 11 ], this paper will focus on constant amplitude loading.

The first group of relationships includes equations that define the connection between crack growth rate ( da / dN ) and nominal stress ( σ ) and/or crack length ( a ); the second group comprises those that relate the crack growth rate to total or plastic strain amplitude ( ε a  or  ε ap ), as well as crack length ( a ). Both groups consist mainly of results from early-stage research and share a major limitation: They lack a parameter that accurately characterizes the mechanical state in the crack tip zone.

When Eq. ( 1 ) is plotted on a double logarithmic scale for constant stress ratio ( R ), temperature ( T ), and loading frequency ( f ), it generates the characteristic curve shown in Fig.  1 , known as the kinetic diagram of fatigue crack growth [ 12 ]. Fig. 1 Kinetic diagram of fatigue crack growth

Excluding the topic of short cracks, the diagram features three distinct regimes. Regime A corresponds to the slow growth phase of the crack; its left-hand asymptote is the threshold value of the stress intensity factor range (Δ K th ), below which the crack does not propagate. Regime B represents stable crack growth, while Regime C marks the region of rapidly accelerating crack propagation; the right-hand asymptote here corresponds to the critical value of the stress intensity factor range or the fatigue fracture toughness (Δ K fc ). Fracture mechanics-based relationships that describe the kinetics diagram can be classified according to which of these three regimes they are able to reflect the crack behavior.

NASGRO model [ 17 ,  18 ] also applies to all three regimes. In Eqs. ( 1 )–( 6 ),  K c  is the fracture toughness,  f *  is an empirical crack opening function,  C m ,  C ,  C p ,  m ,  n ,  p , and  q  are empirical constants.

In general, the broader the range of the kinetic diagram we aim to cover, and/or the more influencing parameters (see Fig.  1 ) we wish to include in the equations, and/or the wider the variety of materials we wish to apply them to, the more complex the formulas become. It is more effective to use a simpler equation within a multiparameter system, allowing a better assessment of the effect of individual factors. In view of this, we decided to use the Paris–Erdogan relationship (3) in this paper, knowing that our testing results mostly correspond to Regime B of the kinetic diagram.

Articles [ 19 ] and [ 20 ] present fatigue crack propagation tests performed on HSLA-80 steel ( R y  = 700 MPa,  R m  = 790 MPa) GMAW welded joints. The crack propagated in the weld metal and in the HAZ, and a single result (Paris–Erdogan exponent) was determined for both locations, as well as for undermatching, matching, and overmatching conditions; specimen and crack orientation were not investigated. Based on the examination of a relatively small number of test specimens, without applying a statistical approach, it was found that the exponent of the Paris–Erdogan equation decreases with increasing strength of the filler metal.

Fatigue crack growth tests were performed on marine steel D32 ( R y  = 390 MPa,  R m  = 507 MPa) and its overmatched GMAW welded joints, using two stress ratios [ 21 ]. Both as-welded and post weld heat treated (PWHT) conditions were examined, so there is only one result (Paris–Erdogan exponent) for each case, and therefore, no statistical approach can be discussed. A significant difference can be observed between the base material and the as-welded condition, but the direction of the change is different for the two stress ratios. There is also a difference between the as-welded and PWHT cases, both for cracks growing in the HAZ and in the fusion zone, which may be due to the overmatching condition.

The authors of [ 22 ] performed fatigue crack growth tests on low-alloyed high-strength steel ( R y  ≥ 685 MPa,  R m  ≥ 785 MPa) designated HG785D and its welded joints. The crack propagated in the weld metal and the HAZ, and two types of joint structures were examined. In one case, the three layers of the joint were made with identical matching filler material, while in the other case, an undermatching-overmatching-undermatching sequence was used. The results (Paris–Erdogan exponent) were determined using two different methods. The two types of weld structure resulted in a difference in the case of cracks propagated in the weld metal, with the “composite” structure being more favorable, but there was no difference in the case of cracks propagated in the HAZ. Significant differences were observed in the methods used to determine the results, which raises the need to use two-stage Paris relationship [ 23 ].

The aim of the present research work is to investigate the two parameters ( C  and  n ) of the Paris–Erdogan equation for different high-strength structural steels and their welded joints and evaluate the effect of the filler metal mismatch phenomenon.

sections.heading: Materials and methods
paragraphs: In this study, five different types of high-strength structural steels, within the 700–1300 MPa yield strength range, were selected for investigation. The materials included the following: S690QL (marketed as Optim 700QL), produced by RUUKKI, S960QL (Weldox 960E), supplied by SSAB, S960M (alform 960M), manufactured by voestalpine, S1100M (alform 1100 x-treme), also manufactured by voestalpine, and S1300Q, an ultrahigh-strength steel with a yield strength of 1300 MPa, for which the producer is unknown.

The mechanical properties, thicknesses, and chemical compositions of these base materials are detailed in Tables  1  and  2 . For most steels, the presented data is based on the corresponding material certificates. However, due to the absence of documentation for the S1300Q grade, mechanical testing and chemical analysis were independently conducted at the University of Miskolc to obtain the necessary material data. Based on the chemical compositions, the carbon equivalents were determined according to EN 10025-1 standard [ 24 ]. All the calculated carbon equivalent values can be seen in Table  2 .

Various filler metal combinations were applied in this study, including undermatching, matching, and overmatching types (and electron beam welding was carried out without filler metal). For all materials except S1300Q, matching filler metals were used. In the case of S1300Q, however, a matching filler metal was not available due to the current limitation in commercial filler metals, which are only manufactured for steels with yield strengths up to 1100 MPa.

In case of welding with filler metal, the used welding procedure was gas metal arc welding (GMAW) with a Daihen welding power source. For welding without filler metal, electron beam welding (EBW) was used. The joints were prepared from plates with dimensions of 350 × 150 mm and thicknesses of 30, 15, or 10 mm, depending on the specific steel grade (as listed in Table  1 ). Butt joints were welded in the PA (flat) position, using X-groove edge preparation for GMAW to ensure uniform stress distribution across the weld and square groove edge preparation for EBW. A backing plate from the same grades as the base material was also used for EBW in single pass with not-through penetration mode to get better result.

Figures  2 ,  3 ,  4 , and  5  illustrate the schematic geometry of the X-groove preparation and the arrangement of welding passes, and Fig.  6  illustrates the square groove. In case of GMAW, a shielding gas mixture of 80% argon and 20% carbon dioxide (M21 type) was applied at a flow rate of 18 L per minute during the welding processes. After welding, fatigue crack propagation experiments were conducted using an MTS 312 universal electrohydraulic testing machine. The control mode used during the tests was load reduction (preload) or constant load amplitude (crack propagation) with a load asymmetry factor of  R  = 0.1 and a sinuous load curve. All tests were performed in a laboratory environment at room temperature. Initially, the loading frequency was set at 20 Hz, which was subsequently lowered to 5 Hz during the final stages of testing. To maintain consistency and ensure comparability across results, specimen preparation followed a standardized procedure for all cases.

To assess crack propagation resistance, three-point bending (TPB) specimens were prepared from the base materials and from all welded joints. The specimen geometry and preparation method for the welded joints are illustrated in Fig.  7 . Fig. 7 TPB specimen locations in welded joint with notch directions (RD = rolling direction)

The notch locations, the notch distances from the centerline of the welded joints, were different; therefore, the positions of the notches and the crack paths represent the most important and the most typical crack directions in a real welded joint. An example for the notch locations can be seen in Fig.  8 . Fig. 8 Notch orientation of TPB specimens used for fatigue crack propagation tests on welded joints of S1100M steel

sections.heading: Discussion
paragraphs: Both the presented and the additional  a – N  curves exhibit similar characteristics for each individual test specimen. The high values of the correlation indexes (close to 1) indicate the reliability and consistency of the conducted tests.

Figure  16  illustrates the relationship between the Paris–Erdogan exponent ( n ) and the constant ( C ) for the tested base materials and their various welded joints. Fig. 16 Connection between the two parameters of Paris–Erdogan equation for the investigated base materials and welded joints

Based on the results there is a close and reliable connection between the two parameters of the Paris–Erdogan equation. Furthermore, there is no significant difference among the materials and their differently mismatched welded joints and different welding processes.

The results shown in Fig.  13  indicate that the T–L and L–T orientations (longitudinal and transverse directions), as well as the T–S and L–S orientations (thickness directions), show similar behavior when considered independently but differ when compared collectively. The tested high-strength steels exhibit distinct fatigue crack propagation characteristics depending on whether the crack advances in the rolling, transverse, or thickness directions. With increasing base material strength, the coefficient of variation shows a decreasing trend for all investigated orientations. The observed variation in standard deviation values, particularly in the thickness direction (T–S and L–S), suggests higher levels of material inhomogeneity in that orientation.

Based on the results shown in Figs.  14  and  15 , crack propagation in various regions of the welded joint collectively provides a statistical representation of the joint’s overall behavior. In both examined directions (21W and  23W), the welded joints exhibit similar trends, with less variation between them compared to the base materials. However, the mismatch effect remains prominent in both orientations. The standard deviation observed in the welded joints is notably higher than that of the base materials, reflecting the increased inhomogeneity of the welded joints. The coefficient of variation values do not show significant differences either between the various mismatch cases or between the two welding processes.

It is unlikely that the investigated welded joints were free from residual stresses. However, it is assumed that the influence of welding residual stresses was not significant in the present study. This assumption is supported by the following considerations. The joints produced by both welding processes were manufactured under conditions allowing free deformation. The GMAW joints were prepared with a symmetric X-groove configuration and welded from both sides using sequential rotation. The EBW joints were produced with high energy density, resulting in a highly localized heat input; consequently, both the weld metal and the heat-affected zone were relatively narrow. All sides of the applied specimens were machined. Furthermore, the presented results focus on Regime B of fatigue crack growth. The influence of residual stresses on fatigue crack growth behavior is generally more pronounced in Regime A, whereas its effect in Regime B is typically less significant.

sections.heading: Summary
paragraphs: Based on the fatigue crack propagation tests performed, several conclusions can be drawn: The applied statistical methodology confirms that the FCG tests are both reliable and reproducible. A clear and consistent relationship was observed between the Paris–Erdogan parameters ( n  and  C ) for both the investigated base materials and their welded joints. Notably, there were no substantial differences found between the base materials and the welded joints in terms of these parameters. The evaluation of the Paris–Erdogan exponent ( n ) reveals that the longitudinal and transverse directions (T–L and L–T), as well as those in the thickness orientation (T–S and L–S), yield similar results individually, though discernible differences arise when considered collectively. The variation in standard deviation across directions suggests a higher degree of inhomogeneity in the thickness direction for both base materials and welded joints. Crack propagation behavior across various regions of the weldment provides a statistically representative characterization of the joints themselves. The two studied directions of the welded joints (21W and  23W) exhibited closely aligned behavior with less variation between them compared to that observed in the base materials. However, the influence of mismatch effect remained a dominant factor in both directions.

From a practical standpoint, these findings support the optimization of filler metal selection for welded structural elements under cyclic loading conditions based on the knowledge of the potentially hazardous areas.

Future work related to this study could focus on increasing the number of specimens within each test group, which would enhance the reliability of the results. Additionally, fatigue crack propagation design curves could be developed based on the statistical distributions of the material parameters ( n  and  C ) for different mismatch characteristics. With the continuous development of the filler metals, further mismatch conditions (matching, overmatching) can be investigated and analyzed.
